On behalf of my party, I should also like to extend our congratulations to the hon. member for Lotbiniere by welcoming him once more to the House, after the Social Credit leadership convention which was a success for him.
His election seems to reflect youth. Indeed, even though he has been in the House of Commons for nine years, the hon. member for Lotbiniere will be only 33 next week. That is in the order of things, Mr. Speaker, for they say that from the demographic viewpoint his constituency is one of the youngest in the country. But in spite of his being young, the new Social Credit leader is one of the senior members in the House, and as the leader of his party in the House of Commons, he acted as a skilled parliamentarian.
He will now have the opportunity to show further evidence of his political talents and we express to him our good wishes. Once more, I congratulate him for his victory and, on behalf of my party, I offer him our best wishes.

Mr. Speaker, on my own behalf and on that of my colleagues, I wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark), and the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) for their kind words, both for myself and for the man in whom all hon. members recognize an outstanding Canadian-the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette).
I am very much aware of the tremendous challenge facing the Social Credit Party of Canada in replacing such a man, but I believe that, over the weekend, we gave the country the picture of a group of serious people, intent upon building this country and cooperating with the others in a spirit of good will. Of course, in politics we have to make electoral gains, and passages of arms are at times inevitable. But there is one thing I have always noticed in this House, that is the solidarity shown by hon. members when time comes to recognize historical facts, as Real Caouette does, in Canada.
I wish to assure all my colleagues, on both sides of the House, that we are eager to cooperate with all hon. members to get on with the business of the House, to continue doing efficient work and making positive proposals in an effort to improve the lot of our fellow citizens.
In closing, 1 wish to congratulate the Leader of the Official Opposition on his fatherhood; he pointed out that the honour of having the youngest leader went from the New Democratic Party to the Progressive Conservatives and now goes to the Social Credit Party of Canada; all this to remind him and all the other party leaders that the Social Credit Party of Canada often has the last word.

subsubtopic: NEW PROCEDURE FOR CREATION OF BANKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am so used to work as a member of a team that I was forgetting my own role.
I should like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. The government tabled in August 1976 a very serious white paper on the decennial review of the Bank Act which, as you know, will soon have to be done. On page 21 of that brief, the government suggests that from now on to become a chartered bank it will no longer be necessary to apply to the Canadian Parliament. It will solely be necessary to obtain letters patent from the Minister of Finance. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is conscious of the fact that it is one of the last powers of Parliament with regard to the banking system and whether he is in a position to answer the House today or
November 8, 1976

seriously consider the matter to give back further powers to Parliament on the banking system instead of withdrawing them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: NEW PROCEDURE FOR CREATION OF BANKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this issue of course has to be debated in the House and in the other place, and I do hope it will be thoroughly considered by all parties in the House. However, 1 would just tell the leader of the Social Credit Party that the aim of this bill is not to give more power to the banks but on the contrary to increase competition, and we hope competition between more numerous banks will benefit savers and borrowers alike. As there will be more banks, we may expect that competition will enable them to make transaction at a lower profit rate.

subsubtopic: NEW PROCEDURE FOR CREATION OF BANKS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the right hon. Prime Minister tell the House how taking power from Parliament could possibly restore competition in the banking system?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we know through experience that when the government is allowed to charter and create banks, there will be more of them than if, each time, we have to go through a very long debate before Parliament which, for inherent reasons, is generally slower in taking action than the government.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST SITUATIONS OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce whom I would like to thank for his co-operation in providing some answers, and the inquiries which apparently he has caused the Chief Statistician to make with respect to Statistics Canada's activities. I want to ask the minister whether he would not agree that we have passed the point where an internal inquiry by the Chief Statistician is the appropriate procedure in view of the way in which the Allan Jeffery affair was handled and in view of the unanswered questions on the activities of other employees and indeed on the efficiency of the department itself. Would the minister not now agree that in order to safeguard the reputation of the overwhelming majority of Statistics Canada employees, an inquiry under the Inquiries Act or by an appropriate committee of this House, even a special one, would be the best method to restore public confidence?

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-379, to amend the Canada Elections Act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO APPOINT ANOTHER ELECTOR AS PROXY VOTER
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO APPOINT ANOTHER ELECTOR AS PROXY VOTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at present, proxy voting is available only to voters who are unable to cast their ballots at the advance polls or on election day because of illness or physical incapacity, because of absence in the course of employment as a fisherman, mariner or prospector, or because of absence while a full-time student at a Canadian educational institution.
This bill proposes to allow proxy voting for voters absent for any purpose, including business, vacation or compassionate travel, and will also eliminate the need for medical certificates for illness or incapacity and the need for a registrar's statement for students. The bill further proposes to allow the urban voter a right presently allowed only to the rural voter; that is, the right of a qualified voter whose name has been omitted from the list of electors to cast his ballot upon being vouched for by an elector whose name appears on the official list of electors.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday before four o'clock I was saying that the government's effort at restraint in the area of CYC, Information Canada and the freezing of family allowances was weak. I suggested there was an enormous potential for restraint in Crown corporations such as Air Canada and the CBC. I was just starting on the Canadian National Railways. I thought it was significant that in an operation like the CNR, where the total revenue was close to $2 billion and the losses on operations in 1975 were $91 million, that the corporation does not even consider that a bill of total interest charges of $111 million could not be cut somewhat as a matter of restraint.
So we have a total deficit for that corporation in the 1975 fiscal year of $168 million, which is an increase of $130 million over the deficit from the preceding year. I hardly think we can consider there is any measure of restraint in that kind of report. There is not only the loss of that income, but also the amount of money that they invest in order to incur that loss. For example, on page 21 of the report of the corporation we see that the government of Canada has an investment of $1.4 billion in the operations of the CNR. Furthermore, there is an investment in shareholders' equity-and the government of Canada is the only one listed in the shareholding section-in the amount of $2.2 billion. The total assets of the CNR now are just less than $5 billion. There is a further example where I think we might see the lack of restraint on the part of this particular Crown corporation. On page 22 of the corporation's report we have this statement in the notes to the financial statement:
-based on the latest actuarial reviews, the unfunded liabilities to be funded over various periods to 2027 amounted to $809,020,329.
They already show a lack of restraint in their statements, but one would wonder why these unfunded liabilities are not shown in the statement instead of only in the notes. This corporation, in addition to its railway operations, has a hotel operation. If we look at page 14 of the annual report, we see that in fact they make a profit on operating their hotels of
Restraint of Government Expenditures $900,000, and also on those they lease to the Hilton hotel organization of $2.7 million, for a total net income for hotel operations of $3.6 million in the year. However, in order to earn that there is a capital expenditure of $4.2 million, so the net cash requirement in that period is something over half a million dollars. If we accept $3.6 million as profit on the hotel operation, we cannot tell what the return on investment is, because the investment of that corporation is not detailed as it relates to particular operations such as hotels. So we have the taxpayers of Canada being asked to contribute to the investment in an operation in which the CNR does not need to be, and this operation is in competition with other enterprises in this country. If the government wishes to be serious about restraint, there is plenty of room in the CNR.
In the remaining time I have, I should like to comment about the Canada Post Office. This should be a place in which we could exercise a little restraint. The gross revenue of the Post Office is $618 million, and the deficit for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1975, was some $321 million. In the preceding year the loss of the Post Office was only $177 million, so these people who are trying to practice restraint have increased the deficit of the department by $144 million. That department spends $1.50 for every dollar it takes in in revenue. The interesting thing about the Post Office is that the statements do not reflect all the costs that are incurred by the Post Office and charged to the Department of Public Works for the occupancy cost of the various buildings the Post Office occupies. It does include an amount for accommodation of $59 million, but on the balance-sheet we see a note at page 8 of the 1975 annual report of the Post Office which says:
Land and buildings are provided and paid for by the Department of Public Works and consequently are not included among the assets. Certain international accounts receivable and payable are not in the balance-sheet since they cannot be established with sufficient accuracy.
Mr. Speaker, I submit there is plenty of room in an operation such as this to exercise some kind of restraint. While I am commenting on the cost of the Post Office that is charged to the Department of Public Works budget, I think it might be well to have a look at that department. In the public accounts for 1976 which were received about a month ago, on page 20.4 we find that in the accommodation program the budget of the Department of Public Works has an expenditure of $252 million for operating expenses for the provision of accommodation of various departments in the government. That may seem like a reasonable figure, but in the previous year that amount was only $220 million. The increase is $32 million, or something like 15 per cent.
Furthermore, the expenditures of the Department of Public Works on capital expenditures including expenditures on works other than federal property amounted to $270 million in that fiscal year-for capital expenditures on buildings they do not even own! That is an increase from $208 million in the preceding fiscal period, which would be an increase of $62 million or something in the order of 30 per cent. In the limited time I have, I want to emphasize that when we are asked to consider a measure of restraint as weak as that we are dealing with, I think it is well for us to insist that more detailed

November 8, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
examination be made of the very many areas available to this government in order to achieve some real kind of restraint.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I always welcome a bill which restrains and cuts back on unnecessary government spending, so I welcome the treasury board's Bill C-19. My only complaint is that it does not go far enough. Included in Bill C-19 is the demise of the Company of Young Canadians. I shed no tears for the CYC. They had their day, but times change and we must now address ourselves to new priorities.
As I said, 1 do not think Bill C-19 goes far enough. There are other areas of government spending that could be examined. I have in mind one which could be called mind-boggling and which, again, deals with CNR, a subject which the speaker before me, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), dealt with. That is another facet of the operations of the CNR. I refer to a picture, with cut-lines, in an Ottawa newspaper.

In an article of the Ottawa Le Droit, November 3, 1976, titled "Publicity Campaign", we read the following:
CN public relations vice-president Jean Cormier administers a publicity budget of $1 million to restore the image of the Crown corporation which, he said, has a reputation of "inefficiency, bureaucracy and waste" because of its association with the government.

That is a rather ludicrous situation when the vice-president of public relations of CNR says he is going to spend, or at least he has, a $1 million budget to restore the image of the CNR; an image which, he says, was created as a result of government policy. So we are giving them money and they are spending the money we give them to restore their image. I suggest that that $1 million could be put to better use. The vice-president of public relations of CNR says he has $1 million to counteract an image. I suggest that if the $1 million is indeed available, it might be better spent in further lowering rail fares so that more people, especially students and young Canadians, could travel across Canada and get to know this country.
Another strange expense that PR people favour is the logo or call it what you will, a trademark, an emblem, a symbol, a design, an insignia, or a squiggly line which reads "CN". These people fall into the trap and they hold the fond belief, apparently, that if you get the right, new logo, everything else will fall magically into place. This morning I made several inquiries through my office about the cost of the CN logo. I found that officials in Crown corporations and bureaucrats are rather reluctant to disclose such costs. I suppose that, like most logos, its cost must have been a source of embarrassment because it seems to be hidden with as much secrecy as the CBC logo was, that new device which was incorporated by the CBC and about which I inquired earlier in the House. So I have not yet been able to confirm the cost of the CNR logo.
(Mr. Clarke (Vancouver Quadra).]
This leads me to the secrecy regarding the expenses of government agencies. In my view, this secrecy is unacceptable. I am repeatedly told, and I cannot accept it, that government agencies and Crown corporations are not required to disclose certain details of expenses relating to internal management and administration. The reason given is that the information might be used by competitors seeking a commercial advantage. I cannot accept that reasoning. When these agencies are subsidized by the taxpayer, I believe the taxpayer has a right to know how his or her money is being spent.
Personally, I think the CNR could improve its image by getting back to the main reason for its being, which is the efficient movement of people and freight as cheaply and as effectively as possible. All the rest is frills-and the expense of frills should not be tolerated by the taxpayer. If, by its own admission, the CNR suffers from an image of inefficiency, bureaucracy and waste, then let it address itself to these problems and the image will take care of itself.
The CNR could be used effectively in the movement of young people from east to west and from west to east. We have had a good beginning in this type of program with the Young Voyageurs, for example, student exchanges, and summer language schools which combine both travel and learning. But these programs have been too limited. Most people do not even know about these programs or their value. However, the programs are very good and should be expanded and enlarged. Lower train fares would enable students and young people to see the country as they travel, and more and better summer language training programs would give students a working vacation that would be stimulating and rewarding.
The cost of the bilingual programs in Canada has also come up for discussion. I think it is important that this money be spent wisely. I point out that I do not criticize the amount of money spent on bilingualism. The time has come, and gone, when we can afford the luxury of debating and toying with the idea of bilingualism, niggling over the cost of it, wondering if we are not moving too quickly, suspicious and fearful of exposing ourselves and our youth to a language and culture that have for too long been alien to us. The time for this has passed, because if we do not accelerate the bilingualism program in our schools, in our communications systems and even in our government services, we are going to face the possibility of losing Quebec and, regardless of whether or not we are ready to admit it, if we lose Quebec we will lose Canada and everything that has made this country worth while.
So what can we do to hasten the day when our two languages and cultures meet and when we talk to one another, instead of remaining in our respective corners brooding and scowling? I submit that we need more in the way of education. I know that the educational system in Canada has always been claimed as the creature of provincial governments. The provinces have guarded their jurisdiction over education jealously over the years, affirming their rights under the BNA Act. But their rights, unquestioned so far, entail enormous responsibilities and duties to give young Canadians the very best education available.
November 8, 1976

In my view, a major part of this education should consist of instruction in the other official language. It should also consist of an introduction to our own cultures and peoples, if only to help our children gain a better understanding of their nation and of its role in the world. In this respect, our educational system and the responsible provincial governments have been negligent. In some cases they have been spitefully negligent. Their attitudes toward bilingualism and biculturalism must change, and they must open their eyes not only to their provincial responsibilities but also to their national responsibilities. If they cannot do this, then perhaps it will be necessary to consider a federal role in education.
Also extremely important to the survival of Canada is the communications field. We are told that we must all be sensitive to the power of the media to shape the public mind and spirit. We are, especially in this House, sensitive to the media. The power-and in it, the wonderful potential-has not been wisely used so far. Instead of a lively system linking disparate parts of the country with information and entertainment from all other parts of the land, we have a loose, unbalanced conglomeration of broadcast centres which look blankly at the rest of the country, hardly aware, hardly seeing. Broadcasting in Canada is ghettoized and balkanized. The media in Canada have not fulfilled what I consider to be their primary role, namely, to introduce Canadians to each other. How can one plead for community understanding, tolerance and compassion, when the members of the national community have never met? The media have the power to take on the role of national communicators. I say they also have the duty to take on this role and that it is long overdue.
Finally, I should like to speak about the development of bilingualism in the federal government and civil service. There is no question in anyone's mind that this is money well spent, that every Canadian has the right to approach his or her federal government in either of the two official languages and to be served in that language. That is little to ask, yet that small but crucial principle has been so widely misunderstood. From this principle let us expand the notion of bilingualism to include more, and much better, language instruction in our shools, and a positive, constructive role for the communications industry in bringing our cultural and linguistic communities closer together.
For too long we have been on the defensive about the policy of bilingualism-almost apologetic-in trying to explain a program which is giving French-speaking Canadians but a smattering of the rights we English-speaking Canadians have enjoyed and taken for granted for years. I suggest that this attitude must be replaced soon with one of justifiable pride in having at least begun the construction of a bridge between what we have been calling the two solitudes.

Mr. Speaker, I think I am the first maritimer to take part in this debate on the son of Bill C-87 from the last session, for want of being able to use somewhat stronger language with reference to its
Restraint of Government Expenditures name. But I will not be the last, because there is an important principle here which very much affects the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Indeed, that principle affects the port of Montreal and other ports on the St. Lawrence river, and it has a substantial effect upon the milling industry in Canada. The policy set forth in this bill is so bad that it has been labelled by one member of the present administration with one classic word. I will indicate later who said it, but I can say now what he said. He said, "It is nuts." When a minister of the Crown, no doubt committed to defence of the bill, has that to say about a measure, it is about time his party and the government he adorns takes another look at the measure.
I intend to devote my speech to the subject of the "at and east rate" and to the matter of the removal of section 272 of the Railway Act; in short, to what clause 15 of Bill C-19 attempts to do. I do so because when the matter originally came up in the spring, the hon. member for Vegreville and myself alternated in bringing the issue, by way of questions, to the ministry. I think at one time we had four or five ministers involved. Then we went to the "late show" to try to make as much noise as we could and to raise the cry of "rape" as much as we could. At least, the bill did not get beyond first reading last session. However, now it has been resurrected. The Frankenstein whose components have not been improved by age, comes before us again.
On Friday the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), the transport critic for my party, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale), the apologist for his party, dealt with the matter of the effect of this measure on grain movement and, more particularly, on the flour industry. I thought the hon. member for Crowfoot, in his usual succint style, put the case pretty well. I thought the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council was being somewhat pessimistic. After all, if the flour industry in Canada is facing some difficulties, we should not forget that wheat is perhaps the one product for which we are known in the rest of the world, and flour is a good commodity with which to help the starving of the world keep body and soul together on this planet.
There is one flour mill near the area I serve. It serves the whole of central Nova Scotia, and it is threatened with closure if clause 15 is passed. As I develop my argument, I think the House will also find that while there was some talk by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) about an alternative program which might restore to the ports what is now so rudely being taken away-at least an attempt is being made-the fact is that he said nothing, and there has been no indication so far that any substantial and workable policy will be substituted.
At one time when the hon. member for Vegreville and myself were using the "late show" to some good effect in getting this subject at least raised as an issue in certain parts of the country, I went to the Halifax waterfront and walked through the mass of sheds there. The floor area of those sheds is about the size of three football fields. I walked between stacks and stacks of flour, stacked almost to the ceiling and

Restraint of Government Expenditures covering, as I have said, an area of almost three football fields. It appeared that alongside there was a Russian freighter loading that flour which I believe was destined for Cuba.
That business is a very important part of the livelihood of the people of the Halifax longshore who have to scratch for a living, and if clause 15 passes, all that would be removed in peremptory fashion by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Transport. The minister should not duck his responsibilities on that one. This measure to repeal section 272 of the Railway Act has all the smell of an action of the Minister of Transport. I will resist it as best I can. My colleagues, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), and the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) will be among the hon. members who will be taking part in this debate, but you can bet your bottom dollar that there will also be hon. members from flour-milling communities in other parts of Canada who will join in the effort. We might even get somebody from the other side in on this effort, because I am going to read some of the quotes which some hon. gentlemen opposite have proffered. This matter is obviously of some concern to them, and perhaps they will participate in the debate along with, I am sure, the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers). He will want to have his say, because this question affects many jobs on the Saint John waterfront, and anyone who represents a waterfront community knows that people do not give up jobs very lightly.
First let us start with somebody who is well known on the government side. He is a long-time friend of mine, and a well known and valuable member of the Liberal party of Canada. He is Mr. J. W. E. Mingo, and he happens to be the chairman of the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Commission. He is a lawyer of standing in the province of Nova Scotia. He is either a past president of the Nova Scotia barristers' society or will be its president in another year or so. He is important in the business life of Nova Scotia; and because money is needed to run an election campaign, he is very important in that he raises money for the Liberal party. In an act of supreme statesmanship, Mr. Mingo sent a telegram to the Minister of Transport in which he said:
Termination of the subsidy and the statutory rates will cost Halifax its export flour trade, estimated at 200,000 tons in 1976, and will greatly reduce the throughput of grain at its elevator, thereby increasing the operating deficit of the elevator to the point where its closure will be inevitable.
Then he makes this point:
Prairie grain moves at statutory rates to Vancouver and Thunder Bay, at an annual loss to the railroads which is now estimated at $150 million or more (and which has to be subsidized by other traffic, including export-import traffic moving to and from the port of Halifax), and from Thunder Bay via the St. Lawrence Seaway at highly subsidized tolls to Montreal, Bay Comeau, and the other river and gulf ports. How is it that this $11 million subsidy on the movement of grain to eastern ports is singled out for termination?
He talked about amounts 14 times as much that are untouched, as far as I can see, by this statute in which the Minister of Transport would say to all of us in Atlantic Canada, "You are only second-class citizens so let's see how I
[Mr. McCleave.)
can turn you into third-class citizens". I have a telegram from Mr. Mingo followed by one from Mr. J. Peill, chairman of the Inter-Cereal Producers Association of Nova Scotia. This telegram was sent to me, and I adopt his reasoning as my own. It reads as follows:
Grain producers of Nova Scotia are concerned with the effect Bill C-87-
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-87 was the father of the present Bill C-19. The telegram continues:
-may have on continued operation of NHB and Dover Mills both of which we consider vital to ascertain continuation and expansion of our young and promising grain production industry in this province.
Modern production methods have made grain production in the past years an economically viable crop in Nova Scotia resulting in doubling of winter wheat acreage for milling purposes every year over the last three.
All signs point to possible continuation of this trend providing handling facilities continue to exist.
Since full implications of Bill C-87 and other contemplated transportation policies are not known we urge that all steps be taken to keep elevator and Dover Mills in operation.
The NHB is the National Harbours Board, Mr. Speaker. I refer to the policy set forth in Bill C-15 as insane. Now I should like to turn to that statesman-like gentleman who used a choicer word-he called it "nuts". In the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, reported in issue No. 84, an exchange took place as follows:

The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) says we should not rely on the Minister of Agriculture, but we can at least put him to the test later and ask whether he intends to stick by the opinion that this clause of the bill is "nuts". We also got rather sympathetic statements in the House from the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), then minister of industry, trade and commerce. Mr. Speaker, I shall be taking part in this debate whenever I can, and helping others with the information 1 have. The file is still quite thick because I have not used much of it, although 1 have touched on the salient points.
It would be a sad day for this House if clause 15 were adopted as law by this parliament. It would be a blow to the people of Halifax and Saint John who work at longshoring and ask why an attempt at government economy should start with them. Why should they be singled out as a working part of the Canadian economy, when they do not have year-round employment for the most part and rely on the flour and grain trade, amongst other things, for their living? For the sake of saving about $12 million we are going to jeopardize the longshoring of Halifax and Saint John: we are going to make a
Restraint of Government Expenditures dent in the business of Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports from which flour and grain are shipped, and we are probably going to put three-quarters of the flour milling industry out of business.
The millers' association has tried to present its case, again getting a sympathetic ear from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Agriculture, but getting the deaf ear of the Minister of Transport.
Sir, it is always good to have economy in government, if you know what you are doing and what the result will be. But I suggest that the present measure will occasion much mischief to the shipping, longshoring and flour sectors of the economy, to say nothing of the farmer who is at the beginning of the line, as it were. I suggest that this attempted economy will do mischief so great that a word the Minister of Agriculture used-"nuts"-will be applied to members of the cabinet if they persist in continuing with this monumental piece of stupidity they are asking us to consider.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we think this is a bad bill, and we oppose it. If we are in economic difficulty, in our view the best solution is to increase production, provide employment and get our economy rolling in high gear. But if the government does not realize all this and feels that it must fall back on a program of restraint, we say that such restraint should at least be practised with some degree of equity and fairness. In our view, this government does not know the meaning of those words when it comes to practising restraint.
I shall illustrate what I mean with some examples. Before I mention them, may I say that I am not at all satisfied with the decision to ditch the Company of Young Canadians and the Local Initiatives Program. I know that the CYC was the brunt of a good deal of criticism. I also know that the young persons who worked under the auspices of the CYC did much useful work coping with social difficulties in this country. It is unfortunate that that project has been ended. Likewise, I was pleased with the number of things done under the Local Initiatives Program to help persons who needed help and could not get it otherwise. I was pleased by the initiative and innovation which that program brought out. The government is to keep the program alive for a while, but plans something else to take its place. That just shows how this government can change its mind in the few months between the time when it introduces a bill and when it gets around to dealing with it.
Information Canada for a long time was a whipping-boy around this House, and it is to go: no longer will it be a whipping-boy. 1 do not think we shall save much money by doing away with Information Canada, and I suspect that many Canadians already miss the services which were available through that agency. I think the main mistake made about Information Canada was that when it was set up the notion was created that it was to take the place of the public relations staffs of the various departments. The idea was that instead of

November 8, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures having every department put out its own press releases, this would all be done by Information Canada.
We discovered that it did not happen that way. The departments increased their public relations activities, and one of the supposed aims of Information Canada was not achieved, instead, Information Canada began publishing material not otherwise available, and opening book stores-all of which I think was good. Because of criticisms levelled at Information Canada from the floor of the House, I suppose the government felt it had no option but to yield to those criticisms and, in the name of restraint, to do away with Information Canada. Now it has gone. Let mine be a voice that is not happy about it.
I move on, sir, to what I think is the main example in Bill C-19 of practising restraint in the wrong place. I refer to the cancellation, for the year 1976, of the escalation of family allowances. The government has been able to say, in effect, "We have saved over $200 million by this means." But it will have been saved mainly at the expense of families and largely at the expense of families in lower income brackets. To me, sir, this is practising restraint in the wrong place. It is making those who can least afford to pay for the government's economy measures pay the larger portion of them.
Let me mention other examples of restraint for which the poor must pay. One such example was brought out particularly in the report of the National Council of Welfare which reached us last week. I confess I was surprised today, after my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some questions about this report, to hear the Prime Minister reply that he had not seen or heard of this document. After all, the National Council of Welfare is an important body, set up and funded by the federal government. It is not some outside agency. It was set up and funded by the federal government for the purpose of making recommendations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on matters of welfare policy.
In the past two or three years it has produced a number of excellent reports which turned the searchlight on inequities and unfairness in our welfare system and society as a whole. The current report, which I hold in my hand, is entitled "The Hidden Welfare System." It is a timely report, coming, as it does, when the government is talking about the need for restraint. The theme of the report, "The Hidden Welfare System," is that the people of Canada are having to pay to certain individuals at least $6.4 million a year because of the unfairness of the exemptions built into our income tax system. This unfairness is documented in this report which is some 40 pages long. The inequity is highlighted extremely well on pages 16 and 17 which tell us how the hidden welfare system works. I do not wish to quote all the material on these two pages, but I will say that these two pages refer to 60 subsidies under the Income Tax Act, with respect to 17 of which the Department of National Revenue provides useful and comprehensive statistics. It is by studying the costs of these 17 subsidies that the National Council of Welfare finds that the treasury is losing, under these exemptions in the Income Tax

Act, about $6.4 billion a year. I should like to read two paragraphs of the report:
An examination of the $6.4 billion cost of the 17 subsidies tells us a great deal about the hidden welfare system. To put this $6.4 billion into perspective, it is equal to well over one-fifth of the entire federal budget in 1974. It was 4'h times the cost of the Olympic Games and 19 times the total new costs of the support and supplementation programs. It was enough money to have provided every family in Canada with an extra $100 per month for food and clothing.
But this $6.4 billion was not distributed equally among Canada's families. The poorest of the poor, those with incomes below the tax-paying threshold, received none of it. For all others the rule was, the higher their income the higher their benefit.
Then follows a table which sets out various income brackets and average benefits received. There are those in the very low brackets who get no benefit at all from the 17 subsidies under the Income Tax Act. For those whose taxable income was under $5,000, the average benefit was $243.75. That sounds good, if you are a low income person. But if you are in the group from $20,000 to $25,000, the average benefit is $1,786.93; and for the group whose income is over $50,000, the average benefit is $3,989.78. Listen to this paragraph, and I am quoting again from the report.
ll would be difficult to imagine any direct and visible government expenditure program which gave $244 to those with income of less than $5,000 but $2,427 ten times as much-to those with incomes of between $25,000 and $50,000, and $3,990 to those who make over $50,000 a year. No government would dare propose such a program. And yet the hidden welfare system does just that, and there is hardly a protest to be heard.
I might add that when there was a protest today from my leader during the question period, the Prime Minister did not even know what he was talking about. I quote again:
The reason the hidden welfare system can get away with it is precisely because it is hidden. The low income taxpayer saving $200 cheers his saving and remains oblivious of the $2,000 saving granted to the person with five times his income.
I might say that in this report it is suggested that if details of all the 60 subsidies or exemptions under the Income Tax Act were obtainable, instead of just 17, it would probably turn out that the total figure would be not $6.4 billion but several billion dollars higher than that. What I am saying is this: if there needs to be restraint, why not practice it here, why not practice it on those who are getting these hidden forms of welfare in the guise of income tax exemptions instead of imposing it on persons who receive family allowances and on the poor generally? It is our contention that the place to practice restraint, the place to practice economy, is where it can be done without hurt to those concerned, instead of where it really hurts our people.
Another question which was asked today raises the whole subject of restraint. My hon. friend from Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) did not get very far, nor did one of the hon. members in the Conservative party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when we ask the Canadian people to cut their expenses and refrain as much as possible from

November 8, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures making expenses which are not urgent, and to abolish useless expenses, I think it is appropriate for the government to bring forward a bill cutting some expenditures which, at a certain time, could appear essential for the good operation of government and for the services offered to Canadians but which after a number of years appear useless and even futile in a few cases because of changing circumstances.
Any good government must endeavour from time to time to direct its efforts to cut wasteful spending which finally becomes a habit in an administration like the federal government and produces expenses which become substantial in the course of the years. Therefore, the object of the present legislation is to ensure that we show the Canadian people a certain will to adjust to the present circumstances.
On December 19, 1975, the President of the Treasury Board announced that certain programs would be abandoned. Certain expenditures which were now useless would be cut, and the federal administration, including the representatives of the people, must show a certain restraint as concerned public spending.
My department was asked, among other things, to see to the disbanding of Information Canada. Originally, the creation of Information Canada was certainly a good idea. This agency rendered many services, especially in the areas most isolated from large centres in Canada. For those who live in large centres like Vancouver, Toronto or Montreal, Information Canada did not bring as many advantages as for the people in isolated centres where government information cannot reach Canadians as effectively. It was in this spirit that Informatinon Canada had been established, but because Information Canada was perhaps not managed as efficiently as possible, and mostly because Information Canada had to face a barrage of repeated and, in a sense, generally negative objections on the part of the opposition, the government had to face the fact that Information Canada could no longer provide Canadians with the same services without provoking increasing criticism. This does not mean that all services previously offered by Information Canada have disappeared. Some of them of course have disappeared, but others have been amalgamated in various departments and continue to meet the needs of Canadians but under other forms.
I would like to report now on what we have done to publish and distribute government publications. As everyone knows, through Information Canada, the government had six bookstores across the country, which operated necessarily in the larger centres and offered their services to a great number of Canadians, but still not to the majority of them.
Moreover, government publications were not, far from it, distributed solely through our bookstores since 65 per cent of the needs were met through the postal service. Therefore, many Canadians are not affected by a change in the distribution of government publications. On the contrary. In addition, because of our labour contracts, it was difficult for our bookstores to adjust to the working conditions in the private sector, that is longer working hours, the opening of our stores at night and on Saturday, when there are necessarily more customers.
[Mr. Goyer.l
After due consideration, we decided to give another orientation to our distribution service through the Department of Supply and Services.
First, we have decided to close our six bookstores which were in operation in six different Canadian cities. In so doing, we will save over $1 million a year and substantially reduce the number of man-years in the government. How will those six stores he replaced? We shall replace them by appointing agents, that is to say by designating private sector libraries that will offer the same services as government libraries, within their commercial activities. In doing so, we shall multiply the number of libraries throughout the country and even in smaller communities where we can find libraries ready to do business with us. We shall multiply the number of service centres throughout the country so that the distribution of government publications be more adequate and reach more Canadians from coast to coast. Furthermore, we shall appoint as government agents all libraries in Canadian universities. It means that every student, every university teacher who use the services of the libraries in our six largest centres will find now similar services in their own university libraries. In doing so, we eliminate annual deficits as well as positions that are becoming redundant.
As concerns the distribution of publication by postal services, we improved that service a lot, as earlier we had to wait from three weeks to one month to receive an order. Our objective is to get it in nine days; it now takes about twelve days, but we hope to reach the nine-day objective within a few months. In doing so, we improve very much what represented 65 per cent of our business volume.
We will also publish very soon a list by subjects of all publications and we shall send this list to special interest groups to avoid sending throughout the country information of no use to the people who get it and so that the people interested can get information on subjects relating to their expertise or their interest field.
In doing so we are going to increase our marketing. We are also going to expand information on government publications and make them available to a greater number of Canadians. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, it may be that some publications will be considered somewhat too expensive by some Canadians. To meet that shortcoming we are sending our publications to all libraries in this country, all those that are registered with the federal government. So there is a legal depository in every library and Canadians can obtain government publications through those libraries without having to spend a penny. For those who insist on doing business with us and buying those publications, once again they will be able to do so from the lists that will be published based on their fields of interest or the expertise sought.
There is a last way which may seem somewhat more attractive for it is surely innovative. We negotiated with CARA which offers various services in several airports in Canada, notably sales services for publications, books on various subjects. So we negotiated with CARA the possibility of having a stand in their bookstores at airports in Canada. So those
November 8, 1976

Canadians using planes in the various airports in this country will now be able to see in those bookstores the latest publications of the federal government and, if they are interested, buy them. So that is an innovation that will surely increase the marketing and profitability of the publications of the government of Canada.
Finally, with respect to decisions we are looking forward to being a lot more active in our efforts to negotiate once again with the private sector the co-edition of some of our publications, notably, of course, in a general way those that are not official publications of the government but that are rather published in the general or particular interest of Canadians. We want to combine with the collections of the private sector.
Why should government publish books in, say, specialized fields such as mining or botany, regardless of collections already in existence in Canada which could very well take in the different subject matters so that, in its publications, the Canadian government be considered on the same level as the private sector? This would further help create jobs in the private sector, one of the government priorities set out in the Speech from the Throne. We would like to enable the private sector to undertake certain tasks for which government has no technical expertise or cannot carry out competitively.

Restraint of Government Expenditures it is on that subject that we are now initiating careful studies to know exactly what would be the necessary corrections to make so that the deficit could be eventually eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, I could give other examples of the measures that we have taken to eliminate certain useless spendings or to restrain government expenditures such as those in the field of computers, when we created pools for buying computers and when we urged the departments to share their use so that the renting of these computers be as cost efficient as possible. Now we are planning to buy certain computers, instead of renting them, and then to rent the computers to the various departments so that we can make the best possible use of our spendings and so that we can use ourselves the renting services.
In the field of photocopying machines, not only in the public sector but also in the private sector, everybody wants to have a photocopying machine very close at hand, something which contributes to increase expenses, henceforth my department will be responsible for making expert services available to all departments so as to make better use of duplicating machines, maximize their output and lower the leasing or purchasing cost of those machines which resulted in heavy expenses for the government and whose costs were not in line with the services they performed.

Those instances have already been mentioned and this will result in many millions of dollars in annual savings because we have put forward a clear and precise policy whereby government services must be provided adequately to all Canadians to meet rapidly their needs. And that is possible by realizing savings and performing more effectively.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are currently asked to use restraint in their wage settlements, to reduce their expenses. Workers and industries are being asked to increase productivity, to work harder to put our economy back on the right course. Various levels of government, whether municipal, provincial or federal, are called upon to take their responsibilities, to reduce unwarranted government expenses, to eliminate waste, to ensure we give Canadians good but efficient and economical services. In this vein, 1 am amazed that in a province where there are now suggestions that the people should eventually separate from the rest of Confederation, that Quebecers are invited to get into absolutely unwarranted expenses in the current economic context.
For instance, urging Quebecers to separate is asking them to grossly overtax themselves to pay for unwarranted expenses. Efforts, talents, time and money are spent and civil servants are at work to undo what the governments are trying to build. In my view that is negative thinking, and Quebecers will have an opportunity to realize this is no time for adventure, this is no time to hire economists or other human resources to do

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 18, 1975, the president of the treasury board announced the elimination of the subsidy on the movement of flour and grain through the east coast ports. This is a very serious move and one which will have devastating and far-reaching consequences. This is in clause 15 of Bill C-19, formerly Bill C-82. If this subsidy should be removed, many aspects of the economy such as the eastern ports, the farmers, inland grain terminals and the flour industry, stand to lose. The scope of this problem is very large indeed. During the last session the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) mentioned the effect the removal of this subsidy would have on the flour industry in Canada. However, Mr. Speaker, let me refresh the memory of members of the House.
First, the removal of this transport subsidy could cause freight rates in some cases to jump by as much as 212 per cent. This is an unrealistic figure, no matter what one happens to be talking about. Second, because of these increased costs, Canada will stand to lose any competitive edge it currently holds in prices, and as a result our flour buyers will be forced to look for alternative suppliers. The alternative suppliers in this case would be the Americans and the European Economic Market. It is interesting to note that both these alternative suppliers already enjoy a competitive advantage with their various export subsidy programs.
Third, the elimination of this subsidy could mean a loss of $28 million, in what economists call the "added value processing activities", with most of this occurring in depressed areas of our country. Fourth, many plants in the milling industry will be forced to close, with lay-offs approaching 3,000 personnel. This figure is for workers directly engaged in the flour industry. Who knows how many workers will be indirectly involved. I ask the government this question: How can you adopt a plan that will increase unemployment when we are already living in an economy where unemployment is over 7 per cent?
Fifth, it is felt that our domestic price of flour will go up because of the number of mills operating at less than full capacity. As one can well see, the removal of this subsidy will have negative results in the flour industry, so much so that the flour industry might be forced into further declines and lose even more of its share of the export flour trade. Of course, there is also the significant effect the reduction in the movement of grain, as a result of the subsidy cut, will have on the eastern ports. This has been discussed in greater detail by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, but let me touch on it briefly. First the removal of financial support for shipments through eastern ports will require increased freight rates. That, in turn, will have the effect of pricing the facilities of
[Mr. Goyer.l
Saint John and Halifax out of business. Naturally, accompanying this will be loss of jobs, loss of markets and reduced rail movements: the list goes on.
However, the biggest injustice here is that at the same time the government announced the plan to eliminate the subsidy to the eastern ports, it also announced that the tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway will not be raised this year, even though this is needed to meet operating costs. The government will subsidize the Seaway and the Great Lake ports, but will let the Atlantic ports fend for themselves.
The third point of discussion, and one which the government has met with weak solutions, is the question of what will be done with this extra 35 million bushels of wheat that is currently handled by the rail movement from these inland terminals to the eastern ports. One solution, as suggested by the government, is the adoption of a new system for moving grains. One that has been discussed is the concept of unit grain trains running from the prairies to Halifax or Saint John. This proposal, however unique-sounding it may be, cannot be considered as a serious alternative. It has never been heralded by the Wheat Board as an alternative mode of grain transportation to the eastern ports. It has never had practical application from the prairies to Halifax or Saint John. It has even been said that the roadbed on which these trains are supposed to be able to travel is not strong enough to support these proposed unit trains full of grain. They will not be able to support any unless a great deal of money is spent improving the roadbed.
The general feeling among the people affected by this proposal is that this extra grain will never see the eastern ports under any other type of grain movement. It is felt that this extra grain is likely to be moved out of the Vancouver port. This is ironic in that the facilities are already overloaded, especially with wheat, and it will not be encouraging to our export buyers if they have heard of the labour unrest there, or are from the other side of the Atlantic. The conclusion that must be drawn from this information is as follows: there may be more efficient and cheaper systems for this movement of grain, but let us carry out our experiments now before we change the present system. Let us find out all there is to know about these alternatives before any present system is replaced or subsidies cut.
Another question to ask in this discussion is: How is it that this particular subsidy is being chosen as the one to be cut? This subsidy, which is in the neighbourhood of about $11 million annually, is quite small and not all that staggering, especially when you compare it to others. For example, $150 million is being spent annually on the subsidy for the movement of grain from the prairies to Vancouver and Thunder Bay. If the government wants to make some savings, simple arithmetic tells you that $150 million is much more than $11 million. This is only one of many examples of grain being moved at statutory rates. There has been no government action to cut any of these rates.
November 8, 1976

Another question, and one that is of particular relevance, is: Why is the public outcry so loud? The reason for this is that the public was never given any indication of the government's intentions before the actual decision was announced on December 18, 1975. After the announcement was made and the people were given a chance to study the consequences, they had every reason for public alarm. It was most evident that very little time or effort on the part of the government had gone into this decision. It seemed that the government had some obscure motive for making this subsidy cut. They certainly had not made a responsible decision, taking into account the government's restraint on transportation programs. It was evident that the subsidy underlying this particular rate was easy to identify, and thus became an easy target for the cut.
It can be said that with the removal of the subsidy and a strict enforcement of the user-pay concept, with no clear alternative policy proposed, the government is abandoning the basic principles of transportation policy, that it should be a tool of regional development and an instrument for national policy. It has also been said that the decision to cut the subsidy was taken before a study of the effect was ever considered. Clear proof of this lack of study is the failure of the government to offer an alternative policy. If a study had been carried out, I am sure it would have shown how disruptive to the Canadian economy will be the action that the government proposes. It would at least have recommended that the subsidy be phased out of existence, not dropped so suddenly. It would have found, also, that despite the restraint objective of this subsidy cut, the end result, with unemployment and disrupted industry, would be increased costs to governments. It would have found that the proposed loss of this subsidy cut to the Canadian economy was estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $100 million. The final comment is that these people and industries must be given a chance to adjust; they do not need this form of shock treatment.
The last point of discussion in respect of the removal of this subsidy, and one that is of great concern to me, is the effect it will have on the inland terminals and on the people who are dependent on the services these terminals provide. The specific terminals in question are those located along Georgian Bay, Lake Huron, Collingwood, Midland, Port McNicoll, Goderich, Owen Sound, Sarnia, Toronto and Kingston. The terminals are presently being used for the movement of grain on the Great Lakes and to the eastern ports. The program in which they take part and which is of interest here is the annual movement of about 35 million bushels of grain by rail to the eastern ports. This movement takes place mainly in the winter months and is subsidized annually to the sum of approximately $10 million to $12 million.
This program is very important to these terminals and makes up most of their winter activity. If it were lost, these terminals would definitely be forced to close in the winter months. With this closure would come the characteristic problems associated with a seasonal industry, everything from the usual labour problems to the more serious problems encountered with the loss of the services these terminals provide. The
Adjournment Motion
whole problem here is that removal of this subsidy and the subsequent closure in the winter months would not be the end result. The end result would be in the indefinite forced closure of these terminals.
Why would the removal of this subsidy cause the terminals to close indefinitely? This is an important question, but one that can be easily answered. The removal of the subsidy will cause decreased activity in the winter months and an over-all reduction of grain movements through these terminals. As a consequence, the operating deficits of these plants will rise until it is no longer profitable for them to stay open. When they reach this point, their doors will close.
Another reason these terminals should not be allowed to close is that these facilities provide a valuable alternative to the St. Lawrence Seaway. If, for some reason, the Seaway was ever forced to be closed or shut down for any period of time, the inland grain terminals could be used to their maximum. Even now they are extremely important during times of strikes or the slowing down of grain movements to Thunder Bay. Another segment of the economy which will be affected by the removal of the subsidy, with its subsequent effect on terminals, is the Canadian grain plan. The farmers of Ontario would suffer a cut in the supply of feed grains.
At present, farmers depend on these terminals for the distribution of the majority of their feed grains. When the terminals close, farmers will be faced with having to find alternative sources of feed grains. These alternative sources will most probably supply the grains at a higher rate. The Quebec farmer who is dependent on feed grain storage at Seaway terminals will also suffer. Terminals further down the Seaway near Montreal and Quebec will not waste any storage capacity on feed grains, instead, they will concentrate only on export grain. The higher price of rail movement of grain will dictate that these terminals accumulate as much export grain moved by water as possible. There will be no room for feed grains. The western farmer will lose the markets which are supplied by grains from eastern ports. This will be the result because of the possible price differential which grain buyers will have to pay in winter months when grain arrives at these ports by train.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes and rental payments of accommodation by tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax up to a maximum allowable of $300 each year.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to propose in this session of parliament a motion seeking tax relief for the already overburdened municipal taxpayer. In reintroducing this motion, I hope to bring to the attention of the federal government, and especially to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the urgent need to alleviate the heavy and intolerable burden of the Canadian taxpayer who is not only heavily taxed today but in most cases is also a victim of double-taxation.
My motion calls for an amount of up to $300 as a deductible expense from federal personal taxable income for municipal taxpayers of owner-occupied homes and tenants renting accommodation in rooming houses or in apartments. We all know that the provision of shelter is a basic one for decent living, and we are also aware of the difficulties today of obtaining adequate and affordable housing with the many services expected and demanded by people in our affluent society, especially in urban and industrialized regions. No level of government acting alone can hope to meet successfully all these demands and needs. That is why all levels of government should be involved in the matter of providing affordable housing and tax relief for the municipal taxpayer.
To be really successful in this task, the three levels of government must co-operate. As the involvement of the federal government in municipal affairs is very limited, due to the provisions of the BNA Act, provincial governments are mostly responsible for education, municipal land use, local economic planning and the provision of many other services to people living in homes in our cities and towns. Unfortunately, not all provincial governments have as yet developed satisfactory policies and programs to ease the financial burden of municipalities. As a result, municipal governments have to tax property owners to raise the money to provide more and more of
