Property taxes have become the major source of money for local governments, making up to 80 per cent of the total municipal revenue, exclusive of transfer payments. In turn, residential property is the main source of property tax revenue for municipalities. However, the many services provided by municipalities, especially education, bear little relationship to the value of one's property holdings, and yet educational costs today comprise from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of our municipal tax bill.
Furthermore, a property tax in isolation cannot meet the ability to pay principle in the matter of taxation, and there is no precise relationship between property ownership and ability to pay. For example, an elderly couple has no great capacity to pay taxes by virtue of owning property. Therefore, property taxes today are considered by many tax experts to be regressive, inflexible, inequitable and bearing heavily upon those who can least afford them. Furthermore, the person paying municipal property taxes is a victim of double-taxation. That is why many countries-for example, the United States-avoid this kind of injustice by allowing property taxes, mortgage interest payments and other expenses as items deductible from personal income tax. On the other hand, Canadian taxation laws allow businessmen to deduct real estate taxes and many operating expenses as items deductible from their income tax.
In the present economic crisis which our country is undergoing, I think it is urgent that the federal government take special measures to reduce unemployment, to control cost of living expenses, and in particular to cut taxes to stimulate the economy. Measures encouraging the construction and purchase of homes would increase the number of jobs and provide a much needed stimulus to our economy. Almost daily we read announcements and predictions in the newspapers that mill rates, hydroelectric rates, water rates and heating costs will be rising again this year almost to intolerable levels in spite of controls and the anti-inflation program. These developments are tragic to people on low incomes, and especially to our senior citizens on fixed retirement incomes. Renters of accommodation in rooming houses and apartment buildings will also face increased rents, as all these services will push up rents in spite of rent controls.
These problems have frequently been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance, and recently by the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities of Canada. The members of this federation expressed great dissatisfaction with the senior levels of government for not giving municipalities sufficient financial assistance to keep down municipal taxes. I am particularly happy that recently the Canadian School Trustees' Association, in a letter to me, expressed their interest in this motion and I would like to read a policy article which that association published at one of its conventions. It reads as follows:
The Canadian School Trustees' Association believes that financial measures should be undertaken by the government of Canada that will permit school-taxes on local property-owners and tenants to be deductible from taxable income.
November 8, 1976

I hope hon. members support such a policy statement. The rumblings of discontent are growing louder each year in all sectors of Canadian society faced with rising costs and heavy taxation, and that is why it is imperative that the Minister of Finance give this matter serious attention. The federal government has already recognized basic tax relief for marital status, dependants, charitable donations, special medical costs, moving expenses, and job-related expenses. Since 1 first introduced this motion in November of 1967, the federal government has increased its total expenditures from $11 billion annually to over $35 billion last year. That amounts to an increase of $24 billion. Therefore, the cost of the program I am proposing should not be entertained by the government or by hon. members speaking in this debate as an excuse for turning it down. I think it is high time the federal government recognized the need to grant Canadians basic tax deduction for shelter. 1 believe that the support and acceptance of my motion this afternoon will help ease the heavy taxation burden carried by our citizens.
I make this motion as a matter of urgent importance and with the serious intention of trying to solve some of the problems of property taxation which have been recognized before now to be inequitable and regressive. Therefore, I hope that this afternoon I will receive support for my motion from all sides of the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rather suspect that the time for the discussion this afternoon will be much too short, because over the past many years I have attended political conventions and policy meetings at the local, provincial and national levels and I know that this subject has come up for considerable discussion. On the face of it, this proposal does sound very attractive, but one has to consider the context in which such proposals have always been presented. Some 10 to 15 years ago when I first dealt with a proposal like this, it was put up, particularly by municipal authorities as an incentive for home ownership.
Civic administrations felt that if they had a higher mix of owner-occupied homes rather than tenant-occupied accommodation in their communities, they would have a more stable population and if the individual was the owner of the premises he occupied there was a greater incentive for him to maintain and improve the property. This was the chief purpose of the proposals 10 or 15 years ago, but it seems to have gone by the board today. The proposals we see are like that made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), designed to alleviate the burden of taxes in this high inflation period. In other words, it is an income-relieving proposition. It is not an incentive program for the owner of property but, rather, is relief against inflationary pressure and ever-increasing taxes at all levels.
The Ontario tax credit provides for a variant of the formula proposed by the hon. member. On the Ontario tax credit return one stipulates the amount of taxes paid during the last taxation year on property owned or rented, and a credit is
Residential Taxes
available. It must be remembered that the hon. member, although his resolution does not say so exclusively, is going for tax credit, not merely a deduction of $300 on taxable income. That would be almost meaningless for all tax credits, whether they be for interest paid on mortgages or on owner-occupied properties. We have seen this proposal many times in this House and outside, and there are various difficulties with it. With all these proposals one has to make up one's mind about the negative consequences.
I think the hon. member said he would grant a credit on owner-occupied residences or to tenants. If he understands income tax law, he will realize that theoretically the tenant has already received the benefit of a tax credit toward that rent, because if there have been expenses with regard to the rent, the owner of the property has been allowed to deduct them and therefore there is, theoretically, already an advantage to the tenant.
But how can each taxpayer be treated equitably? In 1974 my party put forward a proposal that interest rates above 8 per cent, to a maximum of a certain amount, would be deductible from income in order to arrive at a taxable income. But that suggestion had some difficulties with it. It really encouraged the taxpayer to take on a mortgage regardless of the interest rate because he would get credit under the Income Tax Act for anything above 8 per cent. It is the same with the proposals that mortgage interest beyond $5,000 per year, say, would receive some form of subsidy. This is not to encourage ownership but is merely a sort of one-shot affair to alleviate high interest rates. Personally, I do not think that would work; it would be counter-productive.
In this particular instance I wonder whether the benefits that will accrue to the taxpayer will be worth the complexities of the income tax return. With some 18 years' experience on both the government and opposition sides, I know that every exception to income tax leads to greater complexity in the return. It costs a great deal more to administer and it means more trouble and expense for the taxpayer whether the return is completed by himself or someone else. As a matter of fact, a very simple income tax system would be one that taxed revenues at all levels at a flat percentage. It would certainly be an incentive to get out and make more income and develop initiative. On the other hand, for those who are believers of a steeply progressive income tax-and I am not-we start getting exceptions. We have exceptions under the Family Allowances Act. If there were to be the elimination of the child allowance from income tax, it would mean a substantial reduction; at one time estimated almost as high as five points across the board.
There are workers' allowances, moving allowances, allowances for this and for that. As far as corporate income tax is concerned, every exception gives rise to all sorts of difficulties and to greater expense in computation of tax return. I do not think that system necessarily does greater justice in this particular instance, bearing in mind that it is used with some degree of success. I think the hon. member would have added more to his motion if he had included an allowance for

November 8, 1976
Residential Taxes
expenditure of sales tax to see what the total tax burden is on the individual. If the purpose of the motion is to equate the weight of the total tax burden, it is very poor thinking to say that under the Income Tax Act persons earning $5,000 a year shall not pay income tax.
Let us assume that the figure is $5,000. That person may be relieved of the obligation to pay federal income tax; but is he relieved of the obligation to pay municipal tax if he owns a home? Such people may own homes which they bought many years ago when conditions were somewhat different. The owner may have built the home himself and it may be fully paid up. But the point is that the person must still pay his municipal taxes and must also bear as high a load, if not a proportionately higher one, of the retail sales tax burden in certain provinces. Such person must also pay the federal manufacturers' tax-the indirect sales tax which enters into the commodities people buy. Therefore, this proposal will do little to lighten his load.
One hears people speak of low income earners. It is hard to say just who is a low income earner these days, because today people in middle and upper income brackets are living just beyond a bare subsistence level. Only 20 years ago we thought such people were well off.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we ought to consider the total tax package. If the hon. member were to bring forward a proposal covering the total tax package, I think we should be prepared to look hard at it. The hon. member's proposal contains an element of rough justice. Unfortunately, it does not go far enough. I suggest that it would be better to consider the total tax burden borne by the group the hon. member wishes to favour.
In addition, we ought to consider the value of a $300 tax credit to a man paying a marginal tax rate of 50 per cent. One immediately sees the difficulties of applying the tax credit to the varying tax scale brackets. The $300 tax credit is more valuable to a person paying tax at the rate of 50 per cent at the margin than it is to the person lower in the income scale or even, shall we say, to the poor chap who is not paying any income tax. After all, what is the $300 credit worth to the man not paying tax? Absolutely nothing. The cake disappears from the plate before he can eat it. Therefore, we must examine all the factors of this proposal. It is not as easy to resolve as it would first appear to be, and I invite hon. members to give further consideration to the various aspects of this proposal. We are considering a subject which some find it popular to advocate without examining closely its many ramifications. Certainly, a proposal like this could cost the treasury tremendous amounts of money. That is why we must examine its facets in detail to see whether it provides a greater degree of justice than injustice.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) for bringing forward his perennial motion calling on the government to give consideration to allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied

homes and rental payments of accommodation by tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax up to a maximum of $300 each year. This proposal will probably be talked out by the hon. member's Liberal colleagues since it has not been received well by the cabinet, especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet).
I must say the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) treated the meaning of "deductible" somewhat charitably. There is a difference between a deduction and tax credit, and I think the hon. member sponsoring the motion spoke of deductions rather than of tax credits. I suggest that a deduction in this regard would be of little or no use to many people and a tax credit as proposed would be practically useless to those not paying taxes, including pensioners, people on fixed incomes and those earning low and moderate incomes. Perhaps when the hon. member brings forward his motion again next year he will clarify its language and speak of tax credits rather than tax deductions.
Arguments for deductibility are popular and persuasive; yet on close examination one sees that the idea behind them is expensive, regressive and a gimmick which offers little advantage to the average and low income owner-occupier or tenant. Therefore, the hon. member's proposal would be of real benefit only to those high in the income scale, to high income earners and to renters. One could best describe his proposal as prescribing an aspirin for a migraine headache, for he is considering the symptom rather than the cause.
Let us examine more closely the deductibility proposal as put forward by the hon. member. Studies show that such deductibility would be most expensive. I imagine that is why the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs do not support the idea. Allow me to quote the views of William Teron, chairman of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, on this subject as expressed in a recent edition of Executive. He is reported as saying:
As far as deduction of interest charges or taxes, municipal taxes off peoples' incomes, etc., this is an extremely costly program, or would be a costly program. The loss of revenue by government would be something in the order of $1 billion per annum. It would be terribly regressive in that those with larger homes would benefit more than the poorer ones; which is almost in reverse to what society accepts. And we spend something like $200 million-$280 million or thereabouts right now to pay for the subsidies of all the public housing and all the sewerage treatment, etc., that we have done in Canada. And here with one item you would spend four times as much in one year to help all those Canadians who are extremely well-housed, beautifully-housed.
Those Canadians well-housed don't need help. And I believe it is terribly important that we be very selective to help those who don't have good housing.
The attitude of the chairman of CMHC is supported by the government. We contend, as well, that deductibility as proposed is regressive from the point of view of the moderate and low income earner. I suppose I could best illustrate my point by mentioning the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan introduced by the former minister of finance, Hon. John Turner, in the 1974 budget, and passed. That program allows a taxpayer to deduct $1,000 from his income every year up to a maximum of $10,000, provided the money is set aside in a special account and used ultimately to buy either a home or
November 8, 1976

home furnishings. Persons who already own a home are not eligible. As long as the money is to be applied to the purchase or furnishing of a home, it is deductible from income tax and the interest such money earns is not taxed. On the other hand, if the taxpayer decides not to buy a home or furnishings he or she can transfer it to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan and, likewise, avoid taxation. So much for the RRSP program.
Returning to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, in 1974 a subsidy of $65 million was provided. Who gained from that subsidy? Of people earning between $5,000 and $10,000, one in 49 participated in the program. Of those earning between $10,000 and $15,000, one in 32 participated. Of those earning $50,000 or more, one in 16 participated.
The average income earner in the $5,000 to $10,000 bracket received a grant of $264.93. A person earning between $15,000 and $20,000 would be eligible for a grant of $365, a person in receipt of between $20,000 and $50,000 would be eligible for $462, and a person with more than $50,000 could receive $571. Contrast this with the amount available to people with less than $2,000. They got a grant of $105. People getting between $2,000 and $5,000 received $203. That is what happens under a program of this type. To him that hath it shall be given, and from him that hath not, it shall be taken away.
The problems of housing cannot be solved by gimmicks. We have to build homes at reasonable cost. When 1 talk about homes, I am talking about homes for families, rental homes, public housing, non-profit housing. The former minister of state said there were 800,000 people in Canada who paid more than 25 per cent of their income in rent. These are the people we have to help. How is this to be done? By bringing down interest rates.
Last week I made a speech in the course of which I drew attention to what a person pays on a mortgage of $50,000 at the current interest level of 11.5 per cent for a 25-year period. He pays $498 a month, principal and interest. Over the 25-year period total payments amount to $143,000. This is what we have to attack. Surely there is a social responsibility on the part of governments and of all financial institutions to bring down interest rates so that people can buy homes at reasonable costs.
We have to assist tenants by bringing in meaningful measures of rent control and shelter allowances in the case of those on low incomes. We must bear in mind that most people do not pay personal income tax, which is why we must think in terms of shelter allowances rather than tax deductibility. The hon. member for Parkdale was talking about tax credit. But a person who does not pay taxes gets no tax credit whatsoever. It is important that the hon. member distinguish between a tax deduction and a tax credit.
It is time the government attacked the high cost of land. In the year between 1975 and 1976 the price rose from $6,542 to $8,520-that is the average cost of an NHA lot; it increased by 30 per cent in one year. The hon. member comes from
Residential Taxes
Toronto and he knows it is impossible to buy a lot there for less than $30,000, so something has to be done. Mr. Teron, the head of the CMHC, says land costs have behaved very badly and that counter measures will be taken through a land mapping process.
What the government has to do is increase public land banking and release the land at the proper time so that the cost of land is brought down. The hon. member for Parkdale knows as well as I do that the land around the perimeter of Toronto-and this applies to land around the perimeters of almost every major city in Canada-is in the hands of land developers who release it only when it is to their financial advantage. The government should step in, acquire land, and release it at the proper time in such a way as to bring prices down.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) outlined some of the ways in which the provinces are giving help to municipalities. It is true that in Ontario tax credits are available. The system should have wider application. At the moment the limit is $90 but the scheme might well be extended to cover taxpayers with moderate incomes. I believe more tax credits are needed.
I appreciate the fact that municipal taxes are posing an increasing burden. In my view we ought to shift the portion covering education to the provinces and to the federal government-they do pay a certain amount at the moment. But they would have to pay an increased share, more especially on behalf of taxpayers with moderate and fixed incomes.
I cannot accept the proposition of the hon. member for Parkdale that a deduction with respect to owner-occupied homes and rental homes be allowed under the Income Tax Act. But if the hon. member is not successful in persuading the Minister of Finance to put forward his ideas in this respect I hope he will be successful in persuading him to adopt the proposals I have just put forward for a national house building program, a plan to tackle high interest rates, the need to impose greater responsibility on financial institutions, to provide for meaningful rent controls and shelter allowances, and so on. If he does this I shall be very proud of him, but at the moment I am not persuaded of the validity of the proposition he has set forth today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank and congratulate by hon. friend from Parkdale. His proposal was well presented and it was obvious, even without benefit of a chest X-ray that his heart is in the right place.
As a regular member of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, and as one who has received a number of public inquiries on the subject, I greatly appreciate an opportunity to address myself to this subject.
This debate has to do with the need for shelter, one which is considered by many to be a basic human right for the sake of security and privacy. This is the case even in countries with the mildest climates, countries where people can live outdoors the year round if they so choose. How much more vital is it, then,

November 8, 1976
Residential Taxes
to make sure that people are properly housed in a country such as Canada where one can actually perish in the cold seasons, even within shelter, in the absence of related needs such as adequate heating and clothing. This question of survival is acutely aggravated at the present time by such modern tensions as the rapidly rising cost of living, increasing expectations, changing values, social instability, and the energy crisis.
What is the hon. member proposing? He is proposing that property taxes and rental payments be deductible from income tax up to a maximum of $300. I am not sure whether he intended to include mortgage interest payments.
What are some of the main points of the government's position on this subject? First, proposals to allow property tax deductions or credits against personal income tax are usually advocated on one of two grounds. It is sometimes held that such a measure would aid the housing sector. Secondly, it is often held that government should reduce the high cost of housing by enacting such a measure.
The current level of housing starts is over 260,000, seasonally adjusted at annual rates. While this is slightly less than the peak reached earlier in the year, the reduction is not a result of any fundamental weakness in this market but rather a return to sustainable levels of activity. Provision of a measure of this sort is likely to have negligible impact on starts as only a small fraction of the tax savings would be in respect of new units. Any measure of this nature that stimulates the demand side of the market will have the undesirable effect of putting upward pressure on prices and rents and would thus frustrate, to some extent, the efficiency of the measures in reducing housing costs.
As it is highly unlikely that a measure of this sort would have significant positive effects on the housing sector, such a measure becomes essentially a transfer payment. Considerations of equity are thus of primary importance. Judged on this basis, even including the proposed $300 maximum, the proposal of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) does not appear too desirable.
As background to any consideration of the equity of the measure, it should be noted that in recent years the property tax component of the consumer price index has risen no faster than other prices and costs. Against this background it seems fair to say that singling out this component of the recent inflation and subsidizing these particular costs via the tax system is not generally equitable. The government has, via indexing and increases in the federal tax cut, used the tax system in a much broader fashion to compensate those who are hardest hit by inflation.
In addition, if the hon. member for Parkdale is proposing that all rent be deductible up to the $300 maximum, the proposal will be discriminatory in favour of tenants as opposed to homeowners. Equity would require that a percentage of rent, roughly equal to the property tax content of rents, be deductible. Furthermore, a simple deduction or credit approach, as recommended by the hon. member for Parkdale,

would not adequately recognize the income of the recipient. Some reduction in the deduction or credit available, based on the individual's income, would appear essential to ensure that the benefits are directed to those who are hardest hit by increases in housing costs.
While modifications along these lines could be accomplished, any proposal of this nature, regardless of its structure, will involve further inequities. The ultimate beneficiaries of such a general measure will not be those who receive the initial tax deduction. For example, if house prices and rents rise as a result of the deduction, a substantial portion of the benefits would accrue to developers. A measure of this sort makes little allowance for the housing needs of different persons. It could well be argued that larger families require relatively larger dwelling units and thus should be allowed a credit or deduction for a relatively larger fraction of their property tax or rent.
In addition, the inequities between persons residing in different provinces would probably be severe. This would occur because provincial-municipal financing arrangements vary significantly from province to province. In particular, that share of services provided by provinces, and the share of municipal revenues made up by provincial grants, as opposed to property taxes, varies dramatically by province. While this is not a concern to an individual province in structuring its scheme, a federal measure related to property taxes that, of necessity, had a uniform structure across provinces would result in different benefits in different provinces, and would cover a different percentage of the total costs of municipal services in each province. In addition, property tax assessment systems in different provinces differ in their treatment of various types of property. This fact would result in inter-provincial differences in the benefits flowing to various types of housing. The interprovincial inequities resulting from these facts would be substantial.
Several other points are in order in judging the desirability of this proposal. First, as a result of the measure, municipalities could feel less pressure to hold property tax increases down. As a result these taxes could rise, and/or provincial grants fall, from the levels that otherwise would have occurred. This effect would pervert the aims of the proposal and substantially increase the revenue cost. Such a scenario is also not the most efficient way for the federal government to transfer resources to municipalities.
Second, while property taxes are undoubtedly a cost of home ownership, they are levied by municipalities and provinces in order to pay for goods and services. Responsibility for these taxes is a uniquely provincial-municipal affair. Provision of a deduction along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Parkdale might be regarded by provinces and municipalities as an unwarranted federal intrusion into their affairs.
The precise structure that the hon. member for Parkdale has in mind is not clear. In particular it is not clear if he is proposing a deduction from income or a credit against tax paid. While most of the effects noted above would be independent of the precise form of the measure, the revenue
November 8, 1976

cost, and the relative size of tax savings at various income levels would, of course, depend crucially on the structure.
It is estimated that a deduction from tax payable of up to $300 would cost something in excess of $2.5 billion. If the measure were structured as a deduction from taxable income, the cost would be some $500 million. Even with the $300 maximum, a substantial portion of the benefits of such a measure would flow to higher income persons.
The federal government allocates substantial resources to the housing sector. The CMHC budget for new loan commitments is some $1.2 billion. The main portion of these loans will benefit lower income persons. In addition, the expenditures of CMHC for programs such as grants and public housing subsidies is some $300 million. Again a substantial portion of these expenditures, under programs such as AHOP and RRAP, the assisted home ownership plan and residential rehabilitation assistance plan, go to lower income persons. In addition, in 1973 the federal government included municipal school-purpose taxes in the federal-provincial equalization formula. As a result equalization payments are currently some $200 million higher than otherwise. These payments, of course, go predominantly to lower income provinces. It is obvious that all of these existing federal measures provide benefits to those most in need. The proposal of the hon. member for Parkdale, on the other hand, would provide to some extent benefits without regard to need.
What then is the government's conclusion? A measure of this nature does not appear to be desirable. It would not provide significant impetus to the housing sector and would have the perverse and undesirable effect of putting upward pressure on house prices and rents. While the lack of clarity in this proposal makes precise determination of the equity effects difficult, it is the case that the proposal would not impinge equally on persons living in different provinces and it would not adequately account for the different housing needs of families of different sizes. As property taxes have not risen faster than the CPI, subsidizing this particular cost does not appear equitable. The measure would involve a substantial reduction in federal revenues and would not direct benefits to those most in need. Lastly, it would be construed as an invitation to municipalities to raise property tax rates.
In addition, there are a couple of other counter-arguments which have been raised. First, let me compare United States and Canadian tax systems. In response to the argument for a deduction of the expenses on the basis that the U.S. allows it, the following points should be made. It is practically impossible to make meaningful comparisons of personal income tax practices in Canada and the U.S. because of differences in the basic income tax systems. For example, although municipal taxes and mortgage interest on homes are deductible in the U.S., capital gains from the disposal of a home are taxable and the basic personal exemptions are lower in the U.S. than in Canada. While Canada allows a deduction for pension contributions, the U.S. does not. Also, the method of recognizing state and provincial income taxes for federal purposes is different in the two countries. All tax comparisons will have to
Residential Taxes
be made in the context of the total tax structure and the social welfare programs in each country in order to be meaningful.
Secondly, with regard to municipal taxes and mortage interest expense of home owners from a tax policy point of view, one basic principle in Canadian income tax law is that no deduction is allowed in respect of personal expenses. Because the purchase of a home is for personal reasons, such as private living accommodation, no expenses incurred in respect thereof could ordinarily qualify for a deduction under this principle. Although the purchase of a home is a large expenditure, it is no different from a taxpayer's purchase of furniture, clothes or a car. Personally I take issue with that viewpoint but it is one that has been expressed.
These are the main points of the government's position on this subject. However, given the crucial need for shelter in a harsh climate such as Canada's, in a world where shelter should be a minimum basic human right for security and privacy even in areas of the world with an easy climate, the high costs of housing due to speculation and other reasons, and the social importance of stable family life, it behooves any government, and especially one like ours, to recognize persistent public concern for the cost of housing and to give thorough consideration to all suggestions to modify it.
Surely the wit of man, especially the political man, can do that much. This certainly includes the high costs of land, due perhaps to an increasing oligopoly of developers and builders, particularly in dominant urban areas, which are mounting even faster than the costs of buildings themselves.
Whether or not this motion comes to a vote, I urge governments at all levels to give it serious thought. I again commend my colleague, the hon. member for Parkdale, for championing this cause.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment briefly on the motion introduced by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). The House may be assured that I shall not try to kill his motion, because I should like it not to be disallowed. I feel that the issue raised is of paramount importance, although the motion is very moderate, not to say nearly insignificant for the small wage earner,
I have never been able to understand why successive governments have never studied the discrimination which exists between the owner of a single-family dwelling and that of an apartment building. Even now, the owner of a single-family dwelling is unable to deduct a cent of his municipal and school taxes from his income. He must pay 100 per cent of it and, if he borrows to build or repair his house, he must reimburse 100 per cent of this loan, because it is a single-family dwelling. He must pay these taxes twice, while the owner of an apartment building will be exempted to pay two-thirds of his municipal and school taxes, as well as two-thirds of his income tax and of the interests on the money he had to borrow to build this apartment building.
862

November 8, 1976
Residential Taxes
He is continually favoured whereas the person who would need it does not have this opportunity. If this corporation or this individual has enough funds to build up low or high rent apartment buildings, he is favoured, Mr. Speaker, because he is entitled to all those tax deductions. He is entitled to all those deductions whereas the low wage earner wishing to build a house for his family is entitled to none of them. This is the discrimination 1 want to expose to the House tonight.
But they fear depriving treasury of a mere $300. If that makes the tax collector nervous, Mr. Speaker, let us tax a little more those who can afford to pay. It is said that big monopolies, big corporations do not pay more than 25 per cent of the whole taxes in Canada, whereas workers pay 75 per cent. This is asking workers to pay to enrich big monopolies, period.
The motion, although very moderate, should be accepted. As I do not want kill it, I will take my seat immediately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may continue with the remarks I was making at five o'clock when private members' hour was called on Bill C-19, I was talking about the people who would be affected by clause 15 of the bill.
Another segment of the economy that will be affected by the removal of this subsidy, with its subsequent effect on these terminals, is Canadian farming. The farmers of Ontario would suffer a cut in their supply of feed grains. At the present time farmers are dependent on these terminals for the distribution of a majority of their feed grains. When the terminals close the farmers will have to find alternative sources of feed grains. These alternate sources will most probably be at a higher rate.
The Quebec farmer who is dependent of feed grain storage in Seaway terminals will also suffer. The terminals further on down the Seaway near Montreal and Quebec will not waste any of their storage capacity on feed grains. Instead they will concentrate only on export grain. The higher price on the rail movement of grain will dictate that these terminals accumulate as much export grain moved by water as possible. There will be no room for feed grains.
The western farmer will lose the markets that are supplied with grains from the eastern ports. This will result because of the possible price differential grain buyers will have to pay in
November 8, 1976

the winter months when the grain arrives at these ports by rail. Buyers will soon go to other suppliers who can guarantee the same price for grain all year round. The Great Lakes shipping fleet would also be affected when the terminals are forced to close. These ships are responsible for the movement of grain from Thunder Bay to the inland terminals and eastern ports. With the removal of the subsidy they would have to change their traffic patterns, with detrimental results to all concerned.
Presently, because the lower Seaway closes much sooner than the upper lakes in the fall, these grain ships are able to make additional trips to the inland terminals. After these additional trips are made, and in most cases the terminals are filled, the ships then make one final trip. On their return they tie up beside these inland terminals so they can be unloaded later on during the winter months. In the spring the ships docked at these terminals also get an earlier start and are able to make additional runs on the lakes while they are waiting for the lower Seaway to thaw.
With the removal of the subsidy there would be a marked change in the pattern. First of all there would be more movement of grain out of Thunder Bay directly to the eastern export points during the regular navigational season. Again the higher rail rates would dictate that as much grain as possible be moved by water. In the fall the ships will prefer to haul through to the St. Lawrence ports. If they are down through the St. Lawrence they most likely will not have enough time to get back up to the lakehead to load and then winter at the inland terminals.
There will no longer be the rail movement or the docking at these inland terminals, with the end result that there will be decreased activity in the winter. With this decreased activity will come the eventual forced closure of these terminals.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hold the same view as most of my fellow members. The repeal of section 272 should be held off at least one year until the minister can put together his new transportation policy, especially since his predecessor aptly described the existing policy as a mess. Dramatic changes in this one aspect of our national transportation system should not be made without any reference to how this will affect other parts of the economy.
Let me also say that if the government should decide it is desirable to remove the subsidy, it should be removed in such a way that the economy that is dependent upon it can adjust. Also before this political decision is made, we must be sure that all studies on the economic impact of this decision are completed and understood. Finally, should section 272 of the Railway Act be repealed as planned, and no compensating measures undertaken, the economies of the areas affected will be adversely and seriously affected. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this bill should not pass this House until clause 15 of the bill has been removed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Huron-Middle-sex (Mr. McKinley) as he discussed the milling industry.
Restraint of Government Expenditures Coming from the east coast, I too am interested in this. However, I am waiting to hear what the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang), who will be taking part in this debate later, will be saying in the House on the discussions that have taken place in the milling industry, particularly as they relate to the east coast.
My task tonight is to speak on the clauses of Bill C-19 relating to the Department of National Health and Welfare. The government has made known its intention not to escalate in 1976 the rates payable under the Family Allowances Act of 1973. The provisions for this step are encompassed in Bill C-19, and it is in respect of those provisions that I wish to speak today. Before I say anything about the actual provisions, I should like to make a few introductory comments.
No government likes to announce that a program to which it is deeply committed, and in whose worth it strongly believes, will be subject to restraint. Thus these remarks are made with mixed feelings. However, we have recognized, virtually all of us, the need for restraint and for a reduction in the rate of growth of government expenditures. We have all recognized also that all sectors of government activity have to feel the impact of this restraint. Since social programs comprise the largest single portion of government expenditures, it follows that they must bear a share of expenditure reductions.
My investigation demonstrated that the Department of National Health and Welfare had a number of possibilities for restraining the growth of government spending. Measures to restrict the growth of federal government expenditures in respect of the Medical Care and Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Acts had already been put in effect, and no further restrictions in those areas seemed to the government to be immediately desirable.
On the welfare side of the minister's department, and leaving aside the contributory Canada Pension Plan, the largest programs are family allowances, old age security, the guaranteed income supplement for OAS recipients, and social assistance and services expenditures under the Canada Assistance Plan. It was on these programs in particular that the government's attention was focused.
I am told that a reduction or the non-escalation of old age security or guaranteed income supplement programs was not an acceptable alternative. It has been a major part of the social program of this government over the last several years to ensure that benefits payable under income maintenance programs for the elderly reached fully sufficient levels as quickly as possible. To pull back now from the gains that have been made seems to the government to be unacceptable. Either reducing, or not escalating old age security and the guaranteed income supplement would reduce the impact of what has been achieved by the minister and the government. Even given a diminishing rate of inflation, this would doom some of our senior citizens to fall back into grave economic difficulty.
I am told that a somewhat similar argument prevailed with respect to major shared cost welfare expenditures under the Canada Assistance Plan. Under that legislation provincial expenditures on social assistance and services are shared,
80001-551/2

November 8, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures provided the expenditures are incurred on behalf of those in financial need or likely to become in need.
The exact definition of need varies from province to province, but in all cases the federal dollars under the Canada Assistance Program go almost entirely to those with very low incomes. To impose heavy federal restrictions upon these expenditures seemed most inappropriate to the government, and to do so would strike hardest at those least able to protect themselves in difficult economic times.
There were also other reasons for eschewing a major attempt to reduce costs under the CAP. As hon. members are well aware, we are currently nearing the conclusion of a major federal-provincial review of all our shared cost welfare expenditures, a review which it is hoped will result in a major reform and streamlining of the welfare system. Consequently the government thought that this was not the time for unilateral federal action in that field. Of course disbursements to the provinces under CAP are made pursuant to signed agreements between federal and provincial governments which cannot be changed unilaterally without one year's notice. In effect the federal government cannot act quickly without provincial consent.
I think the House will realize that among major welfare programs the federal government would have to consider cost reduction in respect of family allowances. Even here I am told the government moved with great reluctance. The 1975 family allowance level of $22.08 per child is not lavish, but it does provide a substantial measure of income support to Canadian families. Thus for most Canadians with children, the monthly family allowance cheque is an important supplement to family income. The government proposed the non-escalation of family allowances only on the grounds of the very urgent necessity to reduce the rate of increase in government expenditures and on the grounds that among the possibilities for restraint in our major welfare programs the non-escalation of family allowances would cause the least amount of difficulty to Canadians.
The minister has received representations from women's organizations about this decision and, quite correctly, they point out that the family allowance is for many women their only disposable income and the only income over which they can exercise control. The government does recognize this situation in the Speech from the Throne. But it must be reiterated that the decision was made on the basis of effecting a cost saving with the minimum possible detriment to the fewest people.
I should add that those who have been hardest hit by these changes are not left unprotected. Those who can demonstrate financial need will be in receipt of cost shared social assistance payments which do in general rise with the cost of living and which will fill the gap left by the family allowance non-escalation. Those working at minimum wages will, in most provinces, be receiving higher minima this year than last. Those who must utilize unemployment insurance to compensate for temporary loss of employment receive payments based on their wages while they were working. In general those wages are higher this year than last. Moreover, the escalation of exemp-

tions from income tax means that all wage and salary earners in the low and middle income ranges will pay less tax this year than last.
I should add that the reduction of inflation from approximately 11 per cent one year ago to 6.5 per cent in September should clearly have an ameliorating effect on family situations.
I am told that the savings which will be effected, should the House approve these amendments, will be considerable. The statutory payments under the Family Allowance Act in 1975 were almost exactly $2 billion. The non-escalation of payments in 1976 will result in savings of $221 million and will leave expenditures in 1976 at very close to the same levels as those in 1975. In addition, of course, the $221 million annual saving will accrue to the federal treasury in perpetuity since the base for any future adjustment of payments will be the 1975 base year.
The amendments to the Family Allowances Act of 1973 which are laid before hon. members in Bill C-19 are intended to give effect to this non-escalation. There is no need to discuss them in any detail on second reading here today, but I will call hon. members' attention to two features of the amendments. The first is that they are made retroactive to January 1, 1976. In this case the retroactivity provisions are intended to avoid causing additional hardship for Canadians because we have continued since the end of 1975 to pay the 1975 rate of $22.08 per child in order to avoid the problem of overpayments.
The second point to which I wish to draw the attention of the members is that the federal family allowance legislation permits provinces to adopt a different configuration of payments than the federal uniform rate should they desire to do so. Such variations, by age of child, size of family, or both, are permissible provided that the total payments in a province with such a configuration are not substantially more or less than what would have been paid if the federal rate were to apply.
Thus, in addition to giving effect to the Government of Canada's intention to maintain the 1975 family allowance rates through 1976, the amendments which are now placed before the House are intended to permit provincial governments, utilizing their own configurations of family allowance payments, to make the appropriate changes in their own provincial legislation and regulations. The provinces of Alberta and Quebec are the two directly involved. The government of Alberta has agreed to pay the same allowances in 1976 as in 1975 and will adjust its legislation accordingly. The province of Quebec is paying an escalated rate in 1976 but is doing so subject to the clear understanding that the federal government will compensate it only to the level which would have applied had the 1975 rates prevailed. Thus it will be up to that province to make up the difference out of its own treasury.
I would remind hon. members that family allowances were tripled by this government as recently as 1973, rising from approximately $7 previously to $21 by January, 1974, because the government recognized the additional cost to the family of raising children and recognized the important role of the
November 8, 1976

family in the fabric of our society. By means of supplementary legislation these increased benefits for 1974 and subsequent years were escalated to reflect the increase in the cost of living. I would point out that never before were these pensions indexed.
It was a difficult decision for the government to make but in the interests of fiscal restraint, in the social security field as in others, the government opted in 1976 to remove temporarily the escalation factor from family allowances since it was felt that those families in need would have recourse to other social assistance measures. I must underline the word "temporary", however. The legislation before us now refers only to 1976. The Speech from the Throne and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) have stated, and 1 reiterate today, family allowances will again be escalated by indexing starting in January, 1977.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the government proposed these amendments to the Family Allowances Act of 1973 in recognition of the important necessity for restraint-restraint which all Canadians must share. The government believed that this was among the most appropriate and least disruptive means to introduce some restrictions on the growth of social programs.

As I said, this legislation is unsatisfactory. Where the cutbacks are real, such as in the "at and east" rates, the impact will be so detrimental as to create consequential obligations for the government which will far exceed amounts saved. To me, the legislation is an exercise to disguise the government's own extravagant habits and refusal to come to grips with real issues.
I am appalled at the way in which the government can play games with figures when it wants to sell a particular philosophy or policy. The government's instincts for manipulating for political gain never cease to amaze me. You know, there is lots of room for the government to tidy and tighten its own operations. I refer specifically to the way in which the government, its agencies and departments control their internal financing. I do not suppose improvements in this area would attract too much attention in the press; nevertheless, restoring proper financial and parliamentary control is one of the gut issues we face.
The financial control and the management systems of the Government of Canada, its agencies and departments are significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness. Bear in mind that within the Government of Canada, its agencies and departments there is inadequate protection against fraud. Testifying before the Public Accounts Committee, the Auditor General said there is inadequate protection against fraud and we have inadequate mechanisms for determining the extent to which fraud occurs.
A reading of the testimony taken before the Public Accounts Committee reveals that in some departments one can obtain signed blank cheques. One member of the Auditor General s staff who worked on the investigation alluded to the fact that on the very first day of his investigation of the cheque-issuing
November 8, 1976

branch of one department he found signed but unfilled cheques. The department in question issues some two million cheques per month. Also, unless fundamental changes are made, the day may soon come when the Auditor General will not be able to vouch by certificate for the accounts of Canada. If this happened to a corporation whose shares are traded on the stock market, the value of its stock would soon sink to nothing. Or if a small businessman running his business that way were to go to his banker for credit, the banker would tell him to clean up his operation. Unless he could revise the operation, such a businessman could not even get inside the front door of a bank.
I do not know how long the government expects the Canadian people to swallow the blatant inadequacies and devious techniques brought forth before the Public Accounts Committee. In the first volume of the Public Accounts of Canada one sees evidence that the Government of Canada has over-stated its financial position by some $7 million. I see the President of the Treasury Board smiling. Perhaps he thinks it is a joke, a play on words. But the government does not follow consistent and standard accounting practices acceptable to the accounting profession across this country.
The minister knows of my respect for the Auditor General. I think he is bringing some of the inadequacies to light and warning the Canadian people that all is not well with the financial control and management exercised by the government. When can we expect the government to deal frankly with Canadians and adopt an accounting and book-keeping system consistent with generally accepted accounting practices?
When can we expect the government to report on the progress made in carrying out recommendations made by the Auditor General, some 34 in number? I understand the government has agreed to accept 32 of them, but to date there has been no indication of the progress made in this direction. What has happened to these recommendations, recommendations which were endorsed by the Public Accounts Committee? What has happened, for instance, to the recommendation requesting the appointment of a chief financial officer who would oversee the budgeting operations and financial management of all government agencies? I support this concept because under the present system internal management has clearly been lacking. The structure which exists within the Treasury Board and the policing departments of government militates against effective corrective action.
The Treasury Board has not given control measures sufficient emphasis. The estimates and the public accounts, which are the foundation of the control system, have failed to set up adequate standards of accountability. Moreover, under the current system members of parliament are given insufficient information upon which to establish accountability. One could describe this administration as one which is incompetent and which has failed to act as a capable and worthy trustee of

I am sure that in his days in the business world he took care, as one of the prime requisites of his operation, to exercise careful internal management control. I am sure he would want to act in the same way in his present portfolio, but I should like to know what he has been doing since he assumed that elevated position. He is in charge of the cash register and I should like to know how much progress has been made in carrying out the recommendations of the Auditor General. What advice is he giving to his colleagues in this regard? The essence of parliamentary democracy is control of the purse strings. We all know that successive Liberal administrations have not had a good record in this field.
I want to quote from the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts as reported at various dates. This is what Mr. Harris of the Auditor General's Office said, as recorded at page 66 of Issue 45.
Virtually all the observations and recommendations in our report were provided for, to a greater or lesser extent, by the Glassco Commission in 1962. Our recommendations are consistent with Glassco; they vary only in emphasis and degree of detail. The evidence indicates that those responsible chose not to emphasize or implement most of the control-oriented recommendations.
In Issue 47, page 10, we read:
In an environment where the government is not held accountable to parliament, it is less likely that subordinate managers will be held accountable to their seniors. If significant improvements are not made ... in our view little progress will be made in improving financial planning and control within departments and agencies.
In Issue 48 at page 17 the Auditor General is recorded as saying:
It would appear that the statutory provision which is available to Treasury Board is now too little used to guard against departments covering up operating inefficiencies by using funds for purposes different from those originally intended.
Here is another quotation from Issue 50, page 13. Mr. Lafferty is speaking.
It is also our view that until departments introduce effective systems of budgetary control there is no basis for determining whether or not funds are being spent for the purposes, in terms of activities, for which they were provided.
These are stinging indictments of government administration, a stinging indictment of the way in which taxpayers' money has been wasted and pilfered. In a speech during the debate on the address the minister spoke boldly of what he intended to do. He said he would be brutal in taking action with regard to wasteful spending practices. He would tighten up on the taxi slips. Well, that is a step in the right direction. It is about time someone took on this responsibility. But what

November 8, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures is required are basic changes and a fundamental shift in emphasis.
Most important of all is the restoration of parliamentary control. In this connection there must be changes in the form and content of the estimates-another of the recommendations which has been advanced by the Auditor General. What is the Treasury Board doing in this respect? I understand that a study group was established to look into ways and means of modifying the estimates so that they could be more readily understood. Have these changes been agreed upon? Will they be incorporated in the estimates for the next fiscal year? What input, if any, will members of parliament be making? Or will the review be undertaken solely by the bureaucrats?
The minister insists that growth of the public service will be limited to 1.5 per cent this year and one per cent in the next fiscal year. Again this is something of a distortion. It amounts to playing with figures. The use of authorized man hours ; an indication of public service growth is misleading because a large gap exists between the man hours authorized and the actual man hours used. For example in 1975-76 the authorized number of man years for public servants under Treasury Board control was set at 319,000, versus 308,000 for 1974. In the same year actual permanent staff reached about 276,000, versus 260,000 a year earlier. The gap was thus reduced from 15 per cent to 13 per cent. The government claimed, and truthfully, that the growth in authorized man years had been kept below 3.5 per cent, but the actual rate of growth of permanent public servants on staff was double that, about 6.1 per cent.
Projecting this previous 2 per cent drop in the gap between authorized man years and actual man years to 1976-77, the real rate of growth of the public service this year could be 3.6 per cent and not 1.5 per cent, as the government would have us believe. It is certainly fair to assume that this reduction in the gap will take place because the government is making full use of the two ways by which it can be brought about.
In addition, there will be more part time employees used and more consultant and contract workers. The other fact is that Treasury Board has been transferring authorized man years from the department to which they were assigned to a department that has developed a shortage because of over-hiring. I suggest that this playing with figures is very misleading and inaccurate and should not be allowed to take place.
On the administrative side we have a similar experience, and I suspect that it is not being changed as a result of the so-called restraint program. In the last four years some 33,000 new administrative positions have been created, an increase of some 31 per cent. For the 1976-77 fiscal year there are another 3,447 additional positions that have been created. These are the kinds of oddities that occur and which we find very difficult to swallow on closer examination.
Speaking of oddities and peculiarities, 1 want to discuss another matter, Mr. Speaker, which becomes somewhat bewildering as I study the current estimates. It has to do with some
(Mr. Mazankowski.J
departments which overspent rather dramatically, in the section dealing with purchase, repair and upkeep budgets in the 1975-76 estimates, by an amount anywhere from 300 per cent to 400 per cent greater than the amount in the original estimates. The 300 per cent increase over estimates and the 450 per cent increase over the previous year paled into insignificance beside some of the actual increases in departmental budgets.
For instance, the administration branch of the Department of Manpower and Immigration budgeted $36,000 for the item having to do with purchase, repair and upkeep budgets in
1975-	76. The actual expenditure was $4,236,000, an increase of some $4,200,000. This was covered in supplementary estimates A, but what is most noteworthy is that the 1976-77 main estimates forecast a drop to $50,000.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, the forecast expenditure of $2,024,000 for the administration branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare in the 1975-76 main estimates called for an expenditure of only $23,000. The 1976-77 main estimates forecast a decline to $1,235,000. Each of these bears critical examination.
The taxation branch of the Department of National Revenue had forecast expenditures of $6,249,000, against a main estimate of $1,874,000. Again the overrun is covered in the supplementary estimates, but the forecast expenditure for
1976-	77 is down to $1,544,000. The administration branch of the Secretary of State Department had forecast expenditures of $4,719,000 against the main estimates figure of $19,000. That is a difference of $1,700,000 between the amount that was spent and the amount originally forecast. Again this deficiency was covered in the supplementary estimates, but the main estimates for 1976-77 forecast a decline to $331,000, lower but still significantly higher than the estimated figure of $19,000 in the 1975-76 estimates.
The administrative branch of the Department of Supply and Services will spend $1,425,000 against 1975-76 main estimates of $21,000. Again this is covered in supplementary estimates A, but the main estimates for 1976-77 show a reduction to $491,000. The same thing applies to the Department of Transport, which shows a forecast expenditure of $1,858,000 against the main estimates of $112,000 for 1975-76. Some $1,496,000 of this is covered by supplementary estimates, but the 1976-77 estimates show a decline to $1,184,000. The ministry account of urban affairs shows expenditures of $1,085,000, against the main estimate figure of $85,000. Again this is covered in supplementary estimates A, but the forecast for 1976-77 is $130,000.
All these figures indicate, Mr. Speaker, huge spending over-runs under the object, and reduced spending forecasts under the object for 1976-77. What creates special significance in regard to all these figures is the fact that visibly they represent one-time expenditures. Practically none of the departments involved plan to spend anything like the forecast expenditures for 1975-76 in the current fiscal year 1976-77. Indeed the total main estimates for 1976-77 at $14,242,000 for
November 8, 1976

these departments is less than half the expenditures for 1975-76.
I do not know whether we can suggest, Mr. Speaker, that great breakdowns occurred in all these departments, that there was an enormous amount of repairing and servicing required or that these departments tried to use funds through this particular area for use in some other category. We must ask these questions, Mr. Speaker. What buildings or what type of equipment were being repaired? What was the nature of the breakdown? Why was the repair and upkeep not foreseen in the previous year's expenditures? What steps have been taken to improve the departments' ability to forecast such huge expenditures, expenditures that bear no relationship whatever to the original estimate?
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, there are so many ramifications here and possibilities for incompetence that the whole question bears close scrutiny and requires some answers. I hope that the President of the Treasury Board will take a close look at the question and provide the House with those answers. Certainly I intend to follow it up in further questions on the order paper. It is surely an area that bears consideration and I would be prepared to provide the minister with more details if he is inclined to look into the background of these very peculiar figures as they relate to the differential between forecast expenditures and actual expenditures.
1 now turn, Mr. Speaker, to a section of the bill which perhaps is the most contentious, the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act, more commonly known as the "at and east" rates. In 1961 there were four principal reasons for implementing the legislation on the "at and east" subsidy. Number one, to encourage the continued use of eastern ports. Number two, to help keep Canadian flour companies competitive in world markets. Number three, to promote and assist the development and expansion of Canada's grain industry. Number four, to benefit the Canadian economy by providing mill transportation and port employment as well as helping Canada's balance of trade position in manufactured goods.
Those four reasons were valid in 1961 and I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that they are valid today. Certainly there can be no reason why this particular section of the Railway Act should be repealed at this particular time. I am interested to know that both the President of the Treasury Board and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) alluded to the fact that we could be expecting the Minister of Transport to participate in this debate and to outline some new measures that may be implemented as a replacement for this particular provision. If that is so, that should be laid before this House at the earliest opportunity in order that we can not only debate clause 15 to repeal section 272, but also consider the proposed action which the minister is advancing.
I do not know why the minister has chosen not to participate in the debate at this time. I invite him to do so at the earliest possible date so that we can have a look at his proposal. If his
Restraint of Government Expenditures alternative approach is satisfactory, we might curtail or at least shorten the debate to some extent to allow the House to get on to other business.

Of course it goes a little further than that. It is effective on April 1, 1976, or the date on which the act comes into force, whichever is later. We were pleased to get from the government early last summer an undertaking not to proceed with it. So we can assume that the effective date will be the date on which the act comes into force. That will be one of the lengthiest battles which this Chamber has ever seen because this bill will not go through without the most bitter debate that we have seen in a long time. It is a classic unconcern. I continue quoting:
-(ii) To terminate the subsidy, estimated to have aggregated $11 million in 1975, now being paid to compensate the railroads for losses sustained in moving this traffic at statutory rates.
We appreciate that you are acting on the advice of public servants in your department who have given such action consideration. Yet we are at a loss to understand how it can be justified and accordingly we are requesting an opportunity to discuss it with you.
Termination of the subsidy and the statutory rates will cost Halifax its export flour trade estimated at 200,000 tons in 1976, and will greatly reduce the throughput of grain at its elevator, thereby increasing the operating deficit of the elevator to the point where its closure will be inevitable.
I depart from quoting here. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the port of Halifax was built on the principle that this country required a major year round ice-free port on the east coast. That is why it was built 70 or 80 years ago.
November 8, 1976

I again quote:
Closure of the elevator will curtail Halifax's port operation, close down the operations of Dover Mills, and undermine hog production in the province by permitting an increase in the rail rates for the importation from western Canada of domestic feed grains.
Nothing has happened about that yet, has it? To continue:
The justification for such damage to our economy eludes us for a number of reasons including the following:
(1)	Even when it is desirable to remove a subsidy, it is ordinarily undesirable to remove it so abruptly that the economy which relies upon it cannot adjust.
(2)	This is especially true where, as here, the economy is one which the federal government is seeking to strengthen in pursuit of its avowed policy to reduce regional disparity.
(3)	Prairie grain moves at statutory rates to Vancouver and Thunder Bay, at an annual loss to the railroads which is now estimated at $150 million or more and which has to be subsidized by other traffic including export-import traffic moving to and from the Port of Halifax, and from Thunder Bay via the St. Lawrence Seaway at highly subsidized tolls to Montreal, Bay Comeau, and the other river and gulf ports. How is it that this $11 million subsidy on the movement of grain to eastern ports is singled out for termination?
(4)	The explanation is even more difficult when it is appreciated that, in the broad sense, the enormous excess of expenditure over revenue of your department and of the Crown corporations in the transportation field which report to you constitutes a complex framework of transportation subsidies for the benefit of various constituencies of Canadians, and that the only subsidies which benefit the export-import traffic of the Port of Halifax appear to be its share of the one which you now propose to abolish and the operating loss of NHB on its Halifax facilities. This loss was $700,000 in 1975 and is forecast to disappear in 1976.
That is, Mr. Speaker, if we ever get around to some more important legislation than this piece of stupidity.
(5)	We have been informed that your department is reducing its expenditures by $31 million as its contribution to the federal government's program of budgetary restraint, and that, of this $31 million, $23 million, or 74 per cent, including the $11 million subsidy in question, will come from expenditures now being made in the Atlantic provinces. If this information is correct, how is it that the least prosperous region of the country, the one with the most precarious economy and the lowest standard of living, is being asked to bear three quarters of the burden?
Why is that, Mr. Speaker? I am asking hon. members opposite why is that?
(6)	The "at and east" rates were introduced years ago to encourage the use of Canadian ports. So far as we know, encouragement in this manner of the use of Canadian ports for Canadian trade is still the policy of the federal government-
Mr. Speaker, I know of no white paper or no statement to contradict that, yet the government acts differently.
-and, if this is the case, the "at and east'' rates should not be eliminated until a different policy is proposed, debated and adopted. Surely this policy, if it is to be changed, should be changed on its merits, and not for reasons of budgetary restraint.
(7)	To us, it seems that the "at and east" rates were selected for termination, not as part of any well conceived new national transportation policy, but because there was pressure on your department to cut expenditures somewhere and the subsidy underlying these rates was easy to identify and otherwise convenient.
(8)	We suggest that the proper course is to retain this subsidy until the whole question of the movement, east and west, of grain, coal and other bulk commodities is examined from the standpoint of projected traffic, available technology, and cost to the taxpayer . . . When all federal government and railroad subsidies are eliminated, and all technological options are optimized, we suspect the most economical way of moving grain from the prairies to
Restraint of Government Expenditures
Europe will be by rail from Saskatchewan to Halifax utilizing a unit train
composed of special purpose hopper cars.
At all events we would like the opportunity to discuss these matters with you before any irrevocable step is taken.
It would be interesting to know, Mr. Speaker, whether anybody has bothered to communicate with Mr. Mingo with respect to that program. He is a highly respected member of our community, a highly respected member of the Liberal Party of Canada, and a man for whom I have a great deal of personal respect. These are the views he expressed to a government which has frequently in the past sought his advice about political matters in the Atlantic area, particularly in Halifax and Nova Scotia generally.
If the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy) is in the Chamber I should like him to find out whether a response was made to that telegram and, if so, would anyone table it or table a study which sets forth alternatives to dealing with this.
